name: Gumer / Chaha
confidence_why: Banksira 2000 describes Chaha stress as fixed on the penultimate syllable, Völlmin 2017 can neither confirm nor deny this and hears antepenultimate stress in words with an open penult, and Hetzron 1997 holds that stress is not phonologically relevant in Chaha, Ezha, Gumer and Gura at all, while Leslau 1966 and Rose 1997 only say the penult 'seems' to be stressed, so no placement is settled.

catalog_locator: Völlmin 2017 §2.3.4 'Short note on stress', p. 40, with footnote 50 (examples 102-103)
catalog_quote: 2.3.4 Short note on stress According to Banksira (2000: 24), stress (in Chaha) falls on the penultimate sylla-ble, no matter whether the syllable is open (102) or closed (103). (102) acə́nəm ‘he brought’ acənə́xum ‘you (pm) brought’ (103) yə́ngɨd ‘let him touch’ yətmə́rkək ‘let him kneel down’ I can neither confirm nor deny this statement. In my impression the stress in words with an open penultimate syllable falls on the third but last syllable (for example ácənəm). But after all this is only an impression that cannot be proved here. Probably the difficulty in determining the stress bearing syllable lies in the question what exactly counts as stress: pitch or intensity. It could be the case that in Gurage languages these two features do not fall on the same syllable (Ronny Meyer, p.c.). As long as there is no further research on this topic, one has to go with Banksira’s native speaker …
sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Hetzron 1970 'Vocalic length and stress in Ennemor' (Le Muséon 83: 559-581), is about Inor/Ennemor, a separate Glottolog language (inor1238, Peripheral Western Gurage), not seba1251 (Chaha/Ezha/Gumer/Gura, Central Western Gurage). No open copy exists: Peeters Online Journals starts at 1980, archive.org has Le Muséon 75/76/80/82 but not 83 (full-text search returns only citing works), HathiTrust is behind a JS challenge, Google Books (sxULAQAAMAAJ) gives snippets only. Snippets confirm its subject (§0.1 defines Ennemor = Inor, Sar Zəgba subdistrict) and, via Hetzron's own 1977 summary (Gunnän-Gurage Languages §B.1.3, snippet volume 7lVjAAAAMAAJ), its rule: final closed syllable stressed, otherwise penultimate, with complications for final -i/-e and double vowels, which Hetzron only says 'might be the rule in part of the other languages as well'. Read in full text (already held by the project): Hetzron 1997 'Outer South Ethiopic' p. 539, which states that in most OSE languages (i.e. including CWG = seba1251) stress is 'not relevant' and only PWG has a grammatically meaningful system, restating the Inor rule. This refines the catalog's 'descriptions disagree' coding (adds Hetzron's 'not relevant' position; confirms the Hetzron leg is Inor-based, not a Chaha claim) but does not supersede Völlmin 2017 as the deciding source. Priority to acquire: Hetzron 1977 §B.1.3 pp. 42f. high (the only group-level stress discussion covering seba1251's dialects); Hetzron 1970 medium (primary for inor1238, comparative value only here).

new_statements.quote: Stress. In most languages stress, a slight raise of the pitch, is not relevant. Only PWG has a system that is meaningful even for grammar. The following presentation refers to Inor, where these phenomena were investigated in detail. The basic stress rule is: a final closed syllable is stressed; when the final syllable is open, the stress is penultimate: ä-säpärä 'he broke,' yəsäβ'ər 'he breaks'. Final -e, -i are always stressed ... Long vowels and diphthongs behave like a sequence of two vowels: biid 'house', gaara 'loin'. ... Thus, Proto-PWG (still so in Chaha) säpärä-m 'he broke' (≠ subordinate -säpärä) became PWG *säpärä́

new_statements.reading: For the seba1251 dialects (Central Western Gurage: Chaha, Ezha, Gumer, Gura) Hetzron states that word stress is a slight pitch rise that is 'not relevant'; the final-closed-else-penultimate rule with its complications is stated for Inor (PWG, Glottolog inor1238), not for Chaha. This is the only first-hand Hetzron stress statement reachable in full text; it supports keeping the catalog's 'conflict' coding and adds Hetzron's explicit 'not relevant' classification for CWG as a fourth position, distinct from Banksira's penult claim, the Polotsky/Leslau POS split, and Völlmin's hedge.

Chaha is said to retain the Proto-PWG suffix -m rather than the stress contrast. sources.citation: Rose, Sharon. 1997. Theoretical Issues in Comparative Ethio-Semitic Phonology and Morphology. PhD dissertation, McGill University (McGill Scholaris handle 20.500.14905/133483), 309 pp.
sources.quote: 'The stress system of Ethio-Semitic has not been investigated in any detail. Most phonological descriptions state that stress is non-salient or that it follows intonational phrasing. ... Hetzron (1970) discusses Inor stress and vowel length, and declares that closed final syllables or final -i and -e are stressed, otherwise the penult is stressed. In Chaha, it seems as if the penultimate syllable is favoured. In conclusion, Ethio-Semitic stress awaits a more thorough investigation.'

sources.quote: 'B.1.3. Stress The stress system of these languages has ... stress in this domain deals with Ennemor: Hetzron 1970a (568-73). The basic stress rule in this language, which might be the rule in part of the other languages as well, is that a final closed syllable is stressed, and when the final syllable is open, the stress is penultimate. Yet there are complications. First of all, final -i and -e are ... Ennemor (and PWG plus Gura) even further is the fact that the stress is ...' ; '... stress on the preceding more: yəsäß'ər + kw'e 'he will break' (definite ... open syllable, the latter will also be stressed. Thus, the opposition between main and subordinate past in Ennemor ... penultimate vowel is double'
sources.note: The only reachable stress discussion covering the Gunnän-Gurage group as a whole (which includes seba1251's dialects). The rule is stated for Ennemor/Inor and only conjectured ('might be the rule in part of the other languages as well') for the others; one snippet groups Gura (a seba1251 dialect) with PWG for a further complication. So Hetzron 1977 does not state a Chaha/Gumer rule first-hand; the catalog's fn.50 characterization ('his basic stress rule, based on Ennemor, differs from Banksira's rule for Chaha') is accurate but should note that Hetzron did not claim the rule for Chaha.
